5.title: Ashmolean Museum; Sir Arthur Evans: Collections
5.content:
![Image 1: A museum interior with a diverse collection of artifacts and artworks displayed in well-lit glass cases and on pedestals, including pottery, sculpture, and a framed portrait](https://sirarthurevans.ashmus.ox.ac.uk/images/medium/4_0_Image1.jpg)

 View of the Cycladic and Minoan collections on display in the Aegean World gallery at the Ashmolean Museum.

![Image 2: Museum exhibit of artifacts under glass case, with a Minoan bull-leaping fresco replica behind](https://sirarthurevans.ashmus.ox.ac.uk/images/medium/4_0_Image2.jpg)

 View of the Minoan and Mycenaean collections on display in the Aegean World gallery at the Ashmolean Museum.

The Aegean collection at the Ashmolean Museum comprises around 10,000 objects. It is the largest and most comprehensive outside Greece. It contains Neolithic, Bronze and Early Iron Age material from mainland Greece and the islands.

The Cycladic collections, which include several marble figurines and vessels, copper and stone tools, jewellery and clay pots, were largely the gift of Prof. R.M. Dawkins and of the early BSA excavations (1896-1899) at Phylakopi on Melos as well as of A.J. Evans's purchases for the Museum. The Ashmolean houses the largest collection of Aegean seals, rings and sealings and of Aegean scripts outside Greece and of Minoan antiquities outside Crete. The largest part of the Cretan antiquities comes from Sir Arthur Evans's excavations at Knossos and his personal collections from his travels and explorations throughout Crete. It comprises clay, stone and metal vessels, fresco fragments, bronze weapons and tools, jewellery, clay coffins (larnakes) and figurines. Among the most notable assemblages are also the offerings from the Psychro Cave (A.J. Evans excavations) and the Petsofas Peak Sanctuary (J.L. Myres excavations). The collection also includes hundreds of historical replicas and a number of famous forgeries, such as the gems of the so-called 'Thisbe Treasure' and the 'boy-God'. In addition, the Ashmolean holds representative Neolithic and Mycenaean collections, mainly pots and sherds from mainland Greece and the islands.

A major strength of the Aegean collections is the relatively high percentage of provenanced material and the presence of the Sir Arthur Evans and Knossos excavations archives. Both elements present a remarkable opportunity to restudy the material from old excavations. The Aegean collections play an active role in research and in the University

![Image 3: Interior view of an art museum with various archeological relics and a painting of a doctor in a white coat](https://sirarthurevans.ashmus.ox.ac.uk/images/high/4_0_Image1.jpg)

 View of the Cycladic and Minoan collections on display in the Aegean World gallery at the Ashmolean Museum.

![Image 4: The Cretan display at Heraklion Archaeological Museum features a large wall mural and pottery in a brightly lit room](https://sirarthurevans.ashmus.ox.ac.uk/images/high/4_0_Image2.jpg)

 View of the Minoan and Mycenaean collections on display in the Aegean World gallery at the Ashmolean Museum.

4.title: Arthur Evans - New World Encyclopedia
4.content:
[![Image 1: Bronze bust of a man in a suit jacket and tie sits atop a tiered pedestal](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/d/images/thumb/6/6d/SirArthurEvans.JPG/200px-SirArthurEvans.JPG)](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/File:SirArthurEvans.JPG)

Bronze statue of Sir Arthur Evans in The Palace of Knossos, Crete, Greece

Sir **Arthur John Evans** (July 8, 1851 – July 11, 1941) was a [British](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom")[archaeologist](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Archaeology "Archaeology"), who received a knighthood for his work advancing the knowledge of the Bronze Age in the [Mediterranean](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mediterranean "Mediterranean") area. He primarily worked on the island of [Crete](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Crete "Crete"), uncovering ruins and numerous artifacts and artworks from, what he named after the legendary King Minos, the [Minoan Civilization](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Minoan_Civilization "Minoan Civilization"). Among his findings he discovered writings in previously unknown scripts, which he called [Linear A](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Linear_A "Linear A") and Linear B.

Evans purchased land on Crete that contained the ruins of [Knossos](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Knossos "Knossos"), which he excavated and then reconstructed (to the condemnation of purists), producing a [museum](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Museum "Museum") of Minoan [culture](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Culture "Culture"), allowing visitors to have an experience of life in ancient times.

Life
----

Arthur John Evans was born in Nash Mills, [England](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/England "England"). He was the eldest son of Sir John Evans, a paper manufacturer and amateur archaeologist of Welsh descent, who evoked in his son a great interest for [archaeology](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Archaeology "Archaeology"). Evans was educated at Harrow School, at Brasenose College, [Oxford](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford"), and at the University of Göttingen, where he obtained a degree in [history](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/History "History").

In 1878, he married Margaret Freeman, who became his companion and partner in his work until her death in 1893.

After graduation, Evans traveled to Bosnia and [Macedonia](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Macedonia "Macedonia") to study ancient Roman sites. At the same time, he was working as a correspondent for the _Manchester Guardian_ in the Balkans and secretary of the British Fund for Balkan Refugees. However, due to his critical attitude toward local government he made many enemies. In 1882, he was accused of being a spy, arrested, and expelled from the country.

In 1884, he became [curator](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Curator "Curator") of the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford, a position he held until 1908, when he was made professor of prehistoric archaeology. In 1901, he became a fellow of the Royal Society, and in 1911 he received a knighthood. He served as president of the Society of Antiquities from 1914 to 1919, and president of the British Association from 1916 to 1919.

Evans is most famous for his archeological excavations on the island of [Crete](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Crete "Crete"). He visited Crete for the first time in 1894, where an unknown script on seal stones was found together with various unidentified [coins](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Coin "Coin"). After he studied the sites, he proposed that the pre-classical Mycenaean civilization of Greece originated in Crete. He published his ideas in _Cretan Pictographs and Pre-Phoenician Script_ in 1895.

Four years later, for the purpose of excavation, he purchased the site of [Knossos](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Knossos "Knossos"), which became a treasure trove of finds. There, Evans uncovered the ruins of a palace, the restoration of which he worked on for the rest of his life. Following the Greek [legend](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Legend "Legend") of the Cretan King Minos and the beast called [Minotaur](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Minotaur "Minotaur"), Evans coined the name "Minoan" and gave it to this newly found [civilization](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Civilization "Civilization").

By 1903, most of the palace was excavated, revealing the beauty of Minoan artwork, through the hundreds of artifacts and writings that he found. Evans described this work in his four volumes of _The Palace of Minos at Knossos,_ which he published from 1921 to 1935.

Evans continued his excavations until he was 84 years old. He died in a small town of Youlbury near Oxford in 1941.

Work
----

Evans' interest in the island of [Crete](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Crete "Crete"), which according to the Greek [legend](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Legend "Legend") hosted an ancient [civilization](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Civilization "Civilization") of "Minoans," was sparked by [Heinrich Schliemann](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Heinrich_Schliemann "Heinrich Schliemann")’s discovery of legendary [Troy](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Troy "Troy"). Like Schliemann, Evans was an amateur [archaeologist](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Archaeology "Archaeology"), driven by his passion for [mythology](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mythology "Mythology") of the ancient world.

Evans, however, maintained an irrationally obstinate Creto-centrism, which led to unfriendly debate between himself and the mainland archaeologists [Carl Blegen](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Carl_Blegen "Carl Blegen") and Alan Wace. He disputed Blegen's speculation that his writings found at Pylos of [Linear B](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Arthur_Evans#Linear_A_and_Linear_B "Arthur Evans") (the same script Evans found on Crete) were a form of archaic Greek. Evans' insistence upon a single timeline for Bronze Age Greek civilization, based upon his dating of [Knossos](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Arthur_Evans#Knossos "Arthur Evans") and other Minoan palaces, ran contrary to Wace's dating of [Mycenae](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Mycenae "Mycenae"), which saw its heyday in the midst of Knossos' decline. Evans generated strange and convoluted explanations for these findings, and used his influence to have Wace removed from his tenured position at the British School of Archaeology in Athens.

### Knossos

[![Image 2: The Palace of Knossos' ruins with red columns, a staircase, and people are visible on the upper level](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/d/images/thumb/7/78/Knossos_r5.jpg/200px-Knossos_r5.jpg)](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/File:Knossos_r5.jpg)

A portion of Arthur Evans' reconstruction of the Minoan palace at Knossos

Evans believed that King Minos, described in some of the Greek stories, was real, and that [Crete](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Crete "Crete") was the home of a once great civilization. This conviction led him to invest all his [inheritance](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Inheritance "Inheritance"), purchasing a large piece of land that included the ruins of the palace of [Knossos](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Knossos "Knossos"). After unearthing the remains of the [city](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/City "City") and its palace, including the structure of a labyrinth, Evans was convinced that he had finally found the Kingdom of Minos and its legendary half-bull, half-man [Minotaur](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Minotaur "Minotaur").

He published an account of his findings in four volumes _The Palace of Minos at Knossos_ (1921–1935), a classic of [archaeology](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Archaeology "Archaeology"). However, he also substantially restored and partially reconstructed these remains, using foreign materials such as [concrete](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Concrete "Concrete").

While many of his contemporaries were interested in removing items of interest from the sites they uncovered, Evans turned Knossos into a [museum](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Museum "Museum") where Minoan [civilization](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Civilization "Civilization") could become tangible, as he was more interested in building a whole vision of the past than simply displaying its riches. Thus, his reconstructions help the average visitor "read" the site, allowing them to appreciate and enjoy the beauty of the [culture](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Culture "Culture") he uncovered.

### Linear A and Linear B

_Main articles: [Linear A](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Linear\_A "Linear A") and Linear B_

[![Image 3: Upper part of an ancient jug, likely made of clay, featuring a handle on the left and a spout on the right side](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/d/images/thumb/c/c8/Linear_A_vase_filt.jpg/180px-Linear_A_vase_filt.jpg)](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/File:Linear_A_vase_filt.jpg)

Linear A incised on a vase, also found in Akrotiri.

On [Crete](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Crete "Crete"), Evans discovered writings in an unknown script. Though deciphering and translating the scripts found on the site always eluded him, Evans recognized that they were in two scripts, which he dubbed **Linear A** and **Linear B.** He—correctly, as it turned out—suggested that Linear B was written in a language that used inflection.

Linear B was deciphered in the 1950s by Michael Ventris, and found to be an ancient form of [Greek](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Greek_language "Greek language"). Linear A remains an undeciphered script. Its decipherment is one of the "[Holy Grails](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Holy_Grail "Holy Grail")" of ancient scripts.

Legacy
------

Arthur Evans is one of the most well-known [archaeologists](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Archaeology "Archaeology") in history. He was knighted in 1911 for his services to archaeology, and is commemorated both at [Knossos](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Knossos "Knossos") and at the Ashmolean Museum in [Oxford University](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Oxford_University "Oxford University"). The timeline of [Minoan civilization](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Minoan_civilization "Minoan civilization"), which he constructed, although slightly revised and updated, is still considered reasonably accurate. The excavation at the site of Knossos has been continued by the British School of Archaeology in Athens.

Evans used contemporary material to reconstruct the old ruins of Knossos, according to the way he thought the original structures would have looked. This drew serious criticism from contemporary scholars, but Evans was not deterred. He rebuilt what looked like a labyrinth, and built numerous new structures on the old ones, following his own vision of Minoan [architecture](https://www.newworldencyclopedia.org/entry/Architecture "Architecture"). In this way, he blended old and new constructions, such that only a trained eye could see the difference. This practice is strongly condemned by modern archaeologists, although tourists visiting the site enjoy walking through the reconstructions experiencing life at the time of the Minoan civilization, as Evans intended.

------------

Nestor, in Greek mythology
==========================

Enter your search terms: 

Nestor nĕsˈtər [[key](https://www.infoplease.com/key-pronunciation-symbols)], in Greek mythology, wise king of Pylos; son of Neleus and father of Antilochus. In the Iliad, Nestor went with the Greeks to the Trojan War, and although he had lived three generations he was still a vigorous warrior and a respected adviser. In the Odyssey, because of his piety and prudence, the gods allowed him to return unharmed to Pylos after the war.
